title: Measures passed, who lobbied for them, and what the client then received
question: What share of each official’s sponsored measures did a registered lobbyist report raising with officials, and what did the lobbyist’s client receive afterwards?
finding: Of 5,751 measures that passed with a named sponsor, 137 (2.4%) are cited by file number in a lobbyist’s reported contact with a City official. Among sponsors of 50 or more, the share runs up to 6.1% (Sandra Lee Fewer: 18 of 297). The clients on those 137 measures were named as the counterparty in titles worth $89.0 million, and the City paid the same 75 clients $342.5 million in the fiscal years after the first such measure passed, for all purposes. A further 46 sponsor-and-measure pairs match a contact only by subject words, which is an inference and is kept apart.
how: Measures are ordinances, resolutions and motions (appointments left out) that passed and name the official as sponsor: every Board file from 2019 and, before that, the money files, land-use files and enacted ordinances whose sponsors are on disk. A file-number match is a six-digit Board file number that the lobbyist wrote in the report’s file-number box, or after the words “File No.” in the issue line, dated from two years before to three years after the file’s introduction (the rule of the parallel lobbyists analysis); “this official” means the contact names that official, “any” means it names any official or aide. A subject-word match (an inference) is a contact with the sponsor, without a file number, in the six months before introduction to one month after passage, sharing at least two uncommon words with the measure’s short title. For each client: the dollars in the measure’s own title when the client is its named counterparty; the City’s payments to that name in every fiscal year after the fiscal year of passage (the ledger runs from fiscal 2017); and contracts starting after passage. Each client is counted once per official, from the first lobbied measure. Clients who are private individuals are counted but not named, and appeals are shown without their street address. The parallel lobbyists analysis (City dataset “Lobbyist Directory” (DataSF b947-pj2q), generated 2026-11-27) follows the same trail from the lobbyist’s side with the same file-number rule: where it lists a client and measure, its award, permit, contract and before-and-after payment figures are used here instead of being recomputed, and its own count of each official’s lobbied measures (every sponsored measure since 2015, whatever the outcome) is printed in the last columns. See its screens “lobbied-measures”, “sponsors-and-lobbying”, “money-trail” and “after-it-passed”.
limits: Being connected is not being corrupt. The lobbying report form has a box for the file number, and this screen reads it. Most lobbying reports leave the box empty or give a planning case number, so the shares here are floors. A contact asking to monitor, amend or oppose a measure is still a contact. Payments “afterwards” are every City payment to that name for any purpose, most of them under contracts unrelated to the measure; they show that the client does business with the City, not that the measure caused the payment. Subject-word matches can be wrong and are never added to the counts. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
